items.justification: Both assure the security of what is released, A through the development process, B through testing before release.
Timeliness of security updates versus due diligence on external components.
Cryptography for the update mechanism versus contingency planning where no update can be provided.
Physical interface exposure versus maintaining an asset inventory.
Cryptographic strength of authentication versus accessible user guidance.
B requires the system to withstand unexpected inputs and failure generally, which covers A's input validation and demands more besides.
Authentication before network access versus monitoring the internal states of a model.
Prohibiting hard-coded security parameters versus recording where training data came from.
Both protect a remotely reachable interface from misuse, A by requiring authentication, B by applying controls on the API.
Publishing a disclosure policy versus logging system and user actions.
Both restrict the system to what is needed to function, A in code, B in the permissions it holds elsewhere.
Recording why a provision is unmet and running threat modelling on configuration change are separate parts of documented risk management.
Checking for available updates versus monitoring internal model states.
Validation of network input versus verifying that Data Custodian controls were built in.
Reviewed cryptographic implementations versus contingency planning where updates are unavailable.
Uniqueness of security parameters versus notifying users of security updates.
Recognizable model designation versus permissions granted on connected systems.
Limiting unauthenticated disclosure over network interfaces versus security testing before release.
Password generation mechanism versus involving Data Custodians in requirements discussions.
Updateability of software components versus the use of independent security testers.
Brute-force resistance versus publishing a vulnerability disclosure policy.
Disabling unnecessary services versus a threat modelling process naming AI-specific attacks.
Secure development process and threat analysis are distinct processes that together make up a secure development lifecycle.
Presence of a secure update mechanism versus preview access for evaluating model changes.
Both keep a deployed product in a maintained state, A by guiding and informing the user, B by supplying and delivering patches.
Both establish component authenticity cryptographically, A by verifying at boot, B by publishing the hashes to verify against.
Authentication before configuration change versus documentation of design and maintenance plans.
Encryption of sensitive data in transit versus verification that specified controls were implemented.
Code minimization versus documentation of design and maintenance plans.
Cryptography for secure communication versus secure software supply chain processes.
User control over automatic updates versus sharing test findings with operators.
An inbound disclosure route and outbound communication of unresolved threats are the two directions of one external security communication capability.
Cryptography for the update mechanism versus internal channels for disseminating threat updates.
Physical interface exposure versus communication of unresolvable threats downstream.
Management of critical security parameters versus encouraging staff to report risks.
Brute-force resistance versus incident management and recovery planning.
Both keep sensitive material from unauthorized parties, A by encrypting parameters in transit, B by protecting training and test data.
Confirmation that personal data was deleted versus general guidance on system use and configuration.
Cryptography for the update mechanism versus role-tailored security training.
Password generation mechanism versus technical measures supporting human oversight.
